props.title: La Jetée
props.initialSlug: Time travel narrative told through still photos

sections.content: La Jetée (1962) revolutionized experimental filmmaking through Chris Marker's ingenious use of still photographs to tell a haunting post-apocalyptic tale. The film's influence echoes through decades of science fiction, most directly in 12 Monkeys (1995), Terry Gilliam's feature-length adaptation. Marker's 28-minute masterpiece proves how time travel narratives can explore deep emotional terrain through minimal means - just black and white photos, narration, and one breathtaking moment of actual motion. The film's circular structure, where the protagonist witnesses his own death as both child and adult, created a template for complex temporal narratives like Arrival (2016) and Looper (2012).

sections.content: The film's exploration of memory, time, and trauma influenced a wave of philosophical science fiction. Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind (2004) borrowed its meditation on memory and love, while Inception (2010) echoed its layered dream architecture. The protagonist's imprisonment and forced time travel experiments presaged later works like Source Code (2011) and Predestination (2014), where characters are trapped in temporal loops beyond their control.

Marker's innovative visual technique - using still photographs with narration - created a new language for experimental cinema. This approach influenced later hybrid documentaries like The House is Black (1963) and contemporary works like The Salt of the Earth (2014). The film's economy of storytelling through images demonstrates how science fiction can achieve profound emotional impact without massive budgets or special effects. sections.content: Modern filmmakers continue drawing from La Jetée's well. Arrival (2016) adopts its non-linear approach to time and memory. Black Mirror: The Entire History of You (2011) explores similar themes of memory as both salvation and curse. Blade Runner 2049 (2017) echoes its questioning of what constitutes real versus artificial memory. The film's DNA runs through virtually every serious time travel narrative of the past 60 years.
